title: Lewis v. State
description: Whether venue for felony murder charges, where the predicate drug sale occurs in one county and the death in another, should be determined by the location of the drug sale or the location of the death.
plaintiff_argument: Lewis argued that venue was not proper in Gwinnett County because the predicate felony (drug sale) occurred in DeKalb County, and there was no allegation of his actions establishing venue in Gwinnett.
defendant_argument: The State argued that venue was proper in Gwinnett County because it was the location where the cause of death, the ingestion of narcotics, and the res gestae of Lewis's actions resulted.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's order denying Lewis's amended motion to dismiss and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

title: Guy v. Hous. Authority of Augusta
description: Whether a local housing authority, authorized by state statute but activated by city government, is protected from a personal injury suit by sovereign immunity.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Christina Guy, argued that the Housing Authority of the City of Augusta was negligent in providing safety and security, implying it is not protected by sovereign immunity and can be sued.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Housing Authority of the City of Augusta, argued that it is protected by sovereign immunity as an instrumentality of the State, a municipal corporation, or an instrumentality of a municipality, and therefore the personal injury suit should be dismissed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' judgment and remanded the case for further consideration of the housing authority's immunity under the proper common law analytical approach.

title: Bailey v. McKintosh County, Webster v. McIntosh County, McIntosh County v. Webster
description: Whether a zoning ordinance passed by McIntosh County is subject to the referendum procedures of the Georgia Constitution's Home Rule Provision.
plaintiff_argument: McIntosh County argued that its zoning ordinance was passed under the Zoning Provision, not the Home Rule Provision, and therefore is not subject to the referendum process, and that the injunction against its enforcement was improper.
defendant_argument: The Intervenors and Judge Webster argued that the zoning ordinance is subject to the referendum procedures of the Home Rule Provision, and sought an injunction to prevent its enforcement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's order halting the referendum, allowing it to proceed, and affirmed the superior court's injunction preventing the enforcement of the zoning ordinance.

title: Stephens v. State
description: Whether the Georgia statute prohibiting 18- to 20-year-olds from carrying handguns in public violates Article I, Section I, Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Thomas Stephens argued that OCGA § 16-11-126 (g)(1) violates the Georgia Constitution's right to bear arms by prohibiting 18-20 year olds from obtaining weapons licenses and carrying handguns in public, asking the court to overrule its long-standing precedent and apply federal constitutional tests.
defendant_argument: The State contended that the statutory scheme is a reasonable safety measure, not arbitrary, and not a complete prohibition on the right to keep and bear arms, thus a permissible exercise of the police power authorized by the "manner clause" of Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the trial court's dismissal, ruling that Stephens failed to provide a compelling argument to reconsider the court's consistent construction of Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution, thereby upholding the statute.

title: State v. Dias
description: Whether evidence of a defendant's refusal to submit to a warrantless blood test is admissible at trial, with the State arguing for its admissibility and Dias arguing against it based on constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that admitting blood-test refusal evidence does not violate the Fourth or Fifth Amendments or the Georgia Constitution's self-incrimination and search/seizure provisions.
defendant_argument: Dias argues that refusing a warrantless blood test is an exercise of Fourth and Fifth Amendment rights (and Georgia constitutional equivalents) against unlawful search and self-incrimination, and this refusal evidence should not be used against her.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's judgment that excluded the blood-test refusal evidence and remanded the case for consideration of other non-constitutional grounds for exclusion.

title: Republican National Committee v. Eternal Vigilance Action, Inc; Georgia v. Eternal Vigilance Action
description: Whether the State Elections Board (SEB) has the authority to promulgate certain election rules under the Georgia Constitution's nondelegation doctrine and whether various plaintiffs have standing to challenge these rules.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the SEB rules were unconstitutional, unauthorized by the Election Code, violated the nondelegation doctrine due to lack of guidelines, and infringed on the right to vote. They also asserted organizational, associational, and community-stakeholder standing, as well as individual voter standing.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the SEB had sufficient statutory authority and guidelines to promulgate the rules, that the rules did not violate the Federal Elections Clause, and that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the rules.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, reversing the trial court's finding on the Federal Elections Clause and organizational/associational standing, and invalidating four of the seven challenged SEB rules (Reasonable Inquiry, Examination, Hand Count, Drop Box ID) while upholding one (Drop Box Surveillance). It vacated and remanded the issue of Hall's standing as an election board member.

title: Atlantic Games, Inc. v. Georgia Lottery Corporation
description: Whether the General Assembly's delegation of rulemaking authority to the Georgia Lottery Corporation violated the Georgia nondelegation doctrine due to a lack of clear statutory guidance.
plaintiff_argument: Atlantic Games argued that the General Assembly's delegation of rulemaking authority to the Georgia Lottery Corporation lacked clear statutory guidance, violating the Georgia nondelegation doctrine, and requested reconsideration of DOT v. City of Atlanta.
defendant_argument: The Georgia Lottery Corporation implicitly argued that the delegation was permissible and that the case was not a suitable vehicle for reconsidering DOT v. City of Atlanta.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court denied the petition for certiorari in this case.

title: White v. City of Mableton
description: Whether House Bill 839, which incorporates the City of Mableton and creates community improvement districts within it, violates Georgia's Single Subject Rule and precedent by addressing more than one subject matter.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that HB 839 is unconstitutional because it creates "more than one unit of government" (Mableton and CIDs) in a single legislative act, violating the Single Subject Rule and Rea precedent.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argued that HB 839 is constitutional because the creation of Community Improvement Districts (CIDs) is germane and logically connected to the incorporation of Mableton, thus adhering to the Single Subject Rule.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the Appellants' complaint, concluding that HB 839 does not violate the Single Subject Rule or run afoul of Rea.

title: Wasserman v. Franklin County
description: Whether the federal doctrine of third-party standing survives as a means of obtaining standing in Georgia courts.
plaintiff_argument: Wasserman argued that she had standing under the federal doctrine of third-party standing, that Georgia's standing requirements were unconstitutional or preempted for her federal claim, and that Pham assigned his rights to her.
defendant_argument: Franklin County argued that Wasserman lacked standing to assert Pham's equal protection rights.
decision_outcome: The court overruled the precedent that adopted the federal doctrine of third-party standing, concluding that a plaintiff must assert their own legal rights to maintain an action in Georgia courts, and vacated and remanded the lower court's judgment.

title: Sumrall v. State
description: Whether OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) unconstitutionally restricts access to the courts and the right to prosecute and defend one's cause, and whether the trial court erred in dismissing Sumrall's petition for retroactive first-offender treatment due to lack of prosecuting attorney consent.
plaintiff_argument: Sumrall argued that OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) is unconstitutional as it restricts his access to the courts and right to prosecute and defend his cause, and that the prosecuting attorney's inaction constituted implied consent to his petition.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the statute is constitutional, Sumrall failed to obtain the required prosecutorial consent, and therefore the trial court properly dismissed his petition without a hearing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the trial court's dismissal of Sumrall's petition for retroactive first-offender treatment and the denial of his motion to declare OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) unconstitutional.

title: Hollis v. City of LaGrange
description: Whether the trial court has the authority to review claims that municipal utility charges constitute an illegal tax, with plaintiffs arguing the court has such authority and the City arguing it does not due to constitutional restrictions on legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the City's excessive utility charges were illegal taxes not authorized by the Georgia Constitution or law, and the trial court erred in concluding it lacked authority to review their legal claims.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the Georgia Constitution's Paragraph V (d) prohibits the General Assembly from regulating or fixing public utility charges, and by extension, the judicial branch also lacks the authority to review or regulate these charges.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the trial court's judgment, ruling that the trial court erred in determining it lacked authority to review the plaintiffs' claims, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Gonzalez v. Miller
description: Whether the Open Records Act (ORA) applies to district attorneys' offices and whether prosecutorial immunity bars enforcement actions against them, with the plaintiff arguing that the ORA applies and his lawsuit should proceed, and the defendant arguing that her office is not subject to the ORA and she is protected by prosecutorial immunity.
plaintiff_argument: Miller argued that District Attorney Gonzalez violated the Open Records Act (ORA) by failing to produce requested public records and destroying correspondence, and that her office is subject to the ORA, allowing his enforcement action to proceed.
defendant_argument: Gonzalez contended that neither she nor her office is subject to the ORA because district attorneys are constitutional officers of the judicial branch, that Miller lacks standing, and that prosecutorial immunity bars his suit.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of Gonzalez's motion to dismiss, holding that the Open Records Act applies to district attorneys' offices, Miller has constitutional standing, and prosecutorial immunity does not bar official-capacity claims, thus allowing Miller's lawsuit to proceed.

title: Satcher v. Columbia County
description: Whether the permanent injunction granted against Columbia County for stormwater drainage issues was barred by sovereign immunity, and whether property owners could recover damages incurred after providing notice to the county.
plaintiff_argument: The property owners argued they were entitled to a permanent injunction and damages for the county's continuing nuisance and inverse condemnation, including damages incurred after providing notice.
defendant_argument: Columbia County argued that sovereign immunity barred the permanent injunction and that the property owners could not recover damages incurred after notice under OCGA § 36-11-1.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals's opinion regarding the injunction, ruling that the trial court's permanent injunction exceeded the scope of sovereign immunity waiver, and also vacated the grant of certiorari for the property owners' damages petition, effectively denying it.

title: Williams v. Powell
description: Whether OCGA § 16-11-34.1 (a), (f), and (g), which criminalize conduct disrupting legislative meetings, are unconstitutionally overbroad or vague under the Georgia Constitution's free speech protections.
plaintiff_argument: The appellants argued that OCGA § 16-11-34.1 (a), (f), and (g) are unconstitutionally overbroad and vague, violating free speech protections, and that the trial court erred in dismissing their facial and as-applied challenges.
defendant_argument: The appellees argued that OCGA § 16-11-34.1 is not facially unconstitutional, not unconstitutionally vague, and that the specific as-applied claim (Cannon's) failed to show protected expression, distinguishing it from a previously invalidated statute.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, rejecting the appellants' facial challenges to OCGA § 16-11-34.1 (a), (f), and (g) as unconstitutionally overbroad or vague, and rejecting one appellant's as-applied challenge.

title: Cobb County v. Floam
description: Whether the Floams are entitled to declaratory relief regarding the constitutionality of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners' amendment changing commission district boundaries.
plaintiff_argument: The Floams argued that the Cobb County Board of Commissioners' amendment changing district boundaries was unconstitutional, and they were entitled to a declaratory judgment because they faced uncertainty regarding their voting rights and future conduct due to the disputed districts.
defendant_argument: Cobb County argued that the Floams lacked constitutional standing due to no individualized injury and could not obtain declaratory relief because they did not demonstrate uncertainty about their future conduct.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's decision, ruling that while the Floams had standing, they did not demonstrate the necessary uncertainty about their future conduct to warrant declaratory relief, thus dismissing their claim without reaching the constitutional merits.

title: Lovell v. Raffensperger
description: Whether actions seeking declaratory and injunctive relief against state or local government actors must be brought exclusively against the state or relevant local government and in their name, as required by Paragraph V of the Georgia Constitution, to waive sovereign immunity.
plaintiff_argument: Appellants argued that the superior courts erred in dismissing their claims, contending that Paragraph V's waiver of sovereign immunity applied to their actions seeking declaratory relief from acts of the state.
defendant_argument: The trial courts (and implicitly the defendants) argued that the actions were barred by sovereign immunity because the appellants failed to comply with Paragraph V by not naming the State of Georgia or the relevant local governments as the exclusive defendants and in their name.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the superior courts' dismissal of the actions, concluding that the appellants failed to comply with Paragraph V (b) (2) of the Georgia Constitution.

title: In Re: Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission Rules and Code of Conduct
description: Whether the Supreme Court of Georgia has the constitutional power to adopt the draft standards of conduct and rules for the Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission.
plaintiff_argument: The Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission transmitted draft standards and rules for the Court's review and adoption, implicitly seeking the Court's approval and suggesting it has the power to do so.
defendant_argument: The Supreme Court expressed grave doubts about its constitutional power to adopt the standards and rules, citing separation of powers and the nature of judicial versus executive power exercised by district attorneys.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court respectfully declined to take any action regarding the Commission's draft standards of conduct and rules for its governance.

title: Roberts v. Cuthpert
description: Whether the General Assembly waived sovereign immunity and whether judicial immunity was waived for a claim of costs and attorney's fees against a probate judge for denying a weapons carry license, and whether such recovery violates the Separation of Powers Provision of the Georgia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Roberts argued that the General Assembly waived sovereign immunity and the probate judge waived judicial immunity for the costs-and-fees claim, and that recovering such fees does not violate the Separation of Powers Provision because denying a weapons carry license is not a judicial function.
defendant_argument: The probate judges argued that sovereign immunity and judicial immunity barred Roberts's claims for costs and attorney's fees, and that the recovery of such fees was unconstitutional under the Separation of Powers Provision as it infringes on judicial independence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part the superior court's judgment, ruling that sovereign immunity was waived, judicial immunity was waived by the probate judge for the costs-and-fees claim in his official capacity, and the recovery of costs and attorney's fees does not violate the Separation of Powers Provision, remanding the case for a hearing on costs.

title: Raffensperger v. Jackson
description: Whether the Georgia Lactation Consultant Practice Act, which restricts who can provide lactation care for compensation, violates the due process rights of individuals to pursue their chosen profession.
plaintiff_argument: The Act is unconstitutional, irrational, and violates their due process and equal protection rights by preventing them from practicing their lawful profession as lactation care providers.
defendant_argument: The Act does not prevent plaintiffs from pursuing their profession and is rationally related to protecting public health, safety, and welfare by promoting access to quality care.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the trial court's ruling, concluding that the Georgia Lactation Consultant Practice Act is unconstitutional as it violates the plaintiffs' due process rights.

title: In re Judge Christian Coomer
description: Whether the Judicial Qualifications Commission (JQC) has jurisdiction to discipline a judge for conduct occurring before they became a judge or judicial candidate, and whether negligent conduct outside judicial capacity is sufficient for discipline, or if bad faith is required.
plaintiff_argument: The JQC Director and Hearing Panel argued that the JQC has jurisdiction over a judge's conduct that occurred before they became a judge or judicial candidate, and that mere negligence is sufficient to warrant discipline for conduct outside judicial capacity.
defendant_argument: Judge Coomer argued that the JQC lacks jurisdiction over conduct that occurred before he became a judge or judicial candidate, and that discipline for conduct outside judicial capacity requires a finding of bad faith, not mere negligence.
decision_outcome: The court remanded the case to the JQC Hearing Panel, finding that the Panel made two legal errors: applying the Code of Judicial Conduct to pre-judicial conduct and determining that negligent conduct outside judicial capacity could warrant discipline without a finding of bad faith.

title: Session v. State
description: Whether Derrick Session's convictions for failure to register as a sex offender in Georgia should be overturned due to insufficient evidence, violations of his federal rights to travel and equal protection, or a violation of the Georgia constitutional prohibition against legislation regarding the social status of citizens.
plaintiff_argument: Session argued that the evidence was insufficient, the Georgia registration statute violated his federal rights to travel and equal protection by treating him worse than a native Georgian, and the statute facially violated the Georgia constitutional prohibition against legislation regarding the social status of citizens.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the evidence was sufficient, Session's federal rights arguments were based on speculative assumptions, and he failed to show the Georgia registration statute violated the social status provision.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Session's convictions for failure to register as a sex offender, rejecting all his arguments.

title: Johnson v. State
description: Whether a pro se filing made by a defendant who is actually or presumptively represented by counsel is always a legal nullity.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that such pro se filings should not always be considered legal nullities, as this rule can prevent defendants from preserving their appeal rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that pro se filings by counseled defendants are legal nullities, based on past precedent, and raises concerns about counsel's ethical obligations if such filings are allowed.
decision_outcome: The court overruled its past decisions that held pro se filings by counseled defendants are always legal nullities, affirming that courts retain discretion to recognize such filings, and vacated the judgment, remanding the case for the trial court to exercise this discretion.

title: Taylor v. The Devereux Foundation
description: Whether the statutory cap on punitive damages (OCGA § 51-12-5.1 (g)) violates the Georgia Constitution's rights to trial by jury, separation of powers, and equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the $250,000 cap on punitive damages is unconstitutional, violating the right to trial by jury, separation of powers, and equal protection, and acts as an improper legislative remittitur.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the punitive damages cap is constitutional, as the plaintiff failed to prove that 1798 Georgia law authorized punitive damages for "entire want of care" claims, and the legislature has authority to define and limit legal remedies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision to apply the statutory punitive damages cap, reducing the plaintiff's award from $50,000,000 to $250,000, and rejected the plaintiff's constitutional challenges.

title: State v. SASS Group
description: Whether the term "action" in Paragraph V of the Georgia Constitution, which waives sovereign immunity for certain suits against the State, refers to an entire lawsuit or only a specific claim within a lawsuit, thereby determining if a suit naming additional defendants must be dismissed in its entirety.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that "action" means a claim or cause of action, not an entire lawsuit, allowing them to include claims against the State (under Paragraph V's waiver) and other defendants in the same lawsuit, with only the Paragraph V-reliant claims needing to comply with exclusivity.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that "action" means the entire case or lawsuit, and therefore, if any claim in a lawsuit relies on Paragraph V's waiver, the entire suit must be brought exclusively against the State or be dismissed.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's denial of the State's motion to dismiss, vacated the interlocutory injunction, and remanded the case with direction that it be dismissed.

title: Camden County v. Sweatt
description: Whether the special election procedures under the Home Rule Paragraph apply to the Resolutions authorizing the County's purchase of land for a rocket launch facility, with the County arguing they do not apply and the electors arguing they do.
plaintiff_argument: The County argued that the Referendum was not authorized under the Georgia Constitution's Home Rule Paragraph and that the special election procedures do not apply to its resolutions.
defendant_argument: The electors contended that the Home Rule Paragraph authorized the electorate to petition for the repeal of the Resolutions, and Judge Sweatt acted within his authority.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the superior court's denial of the County's petition for declaratory relief and writ of prohibition.

title: Ammons v. State
description: Whether evidence of a defendant's refusal to perform preliminary breath tests and field sobriety tests violates the Georgia Constitution's right against compelled self-incrimination, and whether statutes allowing evidence of refusal to consent to a blood test violate the Georgia Privileges and Immunities Clause.
plaintiff_argument: Ammons argued that using evidence of her refusal to perform breath and field sobriety tests violates her right against self-incrimination, and that statutes permitting evidence of her refusal to consent to a blood test violate the General Assembly's constitutional duty to protect citizens' rights, privileges, and immunities.
defendant_argument: The State argued that evidence of Ammons's refusal to perform tests is admissible and does not violate the Georgia Constitution, relying on prior precedent for preliminary breath tests and asserting that the Privileges and Immunities Clause does not bar admission of blood test refusal evidence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, ruling that evidence of refusal to perform preliminary breath and field sobriety tests is inadmissible, but evidence of refusal to consent to a blood test is admissible.

title: Reed v. State
description: Whether Jaquavious Reed's conviction for murder and other charges should be overturned due to alleged errors including insufficient evidence, appellate delay, denial of right to be present, prosecutorial conflict, incomplete transcript, Brady violation, denial of continuance, ineffective assistance of counsel, and improper sentencing.
plaintiff_argument: Reed argued his conviction should be overturned due to insufficient evidence, inordinate appellate delay, denial of his right to be present at bench conferences, a conflict of interest with the DA's office, an incomplete trial transcript, a Brady violation, denial of a continuance for a surprise witness, ineffective assistance of counsel, and improper sentencing.
defendant_argument: The State argued the evidence was sufficient, Reed failed to show prejudice from appellate delay or incomplete transcript, his right to be present was not violated or was waived, the conflict of interest claim was waived, there was no Brady violation, and the denial of continuance was not an abuse of discretion, while conceding the improper sentencing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Reed's conviction for malice murder, vacated his conviction for felony murder, and remanded the case for resentencing, denying all other claims for overturning the conviction.

title: Prickett v. State
description: Whether the trial court erred in denying Prickett's motion for a new trial based on claims of ineffective assistance of counsel, violation of his right to be present, and prosecutorial misconduct, and whether Prickett's convictions and sentences should be vacated.
plaintiff_argument: Prickett argued that the trial court erred by denying his motion for a new trial due to ineffective assistance of counsel, violation of his right to be present, and failure to address prosecutorial misconduct, and that his convictions and sentences should be vacated.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the trial court correctly denied the motion for a new trial as there was no prejudice or constitutional violation, and that the convictions were valid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of Prickett's motion for a new trial but vacated his convictions and sentences, remanding the case for resentencing due to errors in the original sentencing.

title: Awad v. State
description: Whether Paragraph XVI of the Georgia Constitution prohibits the State from admitting into evidence a defendant's refusal to submit to a state-administered urine test for chemical testing, on the grounds that it violates the right against compelled self-incrimination.
plaintiff_argument: Awad argued that the right against compelled self-incrimination protected by Paragraph XVI of the Georgia Constitution prohibits the State from admitting evidence of his refusal to submit to a urine test, as providing a urine sample in a collection container requires an affirmative act that generates self-incriminating evidence.
defendant_argument: The State argued that obtaining a urine sample does not implicate the right against compelled self-incrimination because it does not require an 'act' on the part of the defendant, comparing it to other bodily substances like DNA or blood, and that commenting on refusal does not necessarily implicate rights under Paragraph XVI.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the trial court properly suppressed evidence of Awad's refusal to submit to a urine test, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Harvey v. Merchan
description: Whether OCGA § 9-3-33.1, which revives time-barred civil claims for childhood sexual abuse, can apply to acts that occurred outside of Georgia and whether its retroactive application violates Georgia's constitutional ban on retroactive laws or federal and state due process and equal protection clauses.
plaintiff_argument: Merchan argued that OCGA § 9-3-33.1 should apply to revive her claims, including those for abuse that occurred in Quebec, and that the statute is constitutional, not violating prohibitions against retroactive laws or due process/equal protection.
defendant_argument: The Harveys argued that Merchan's claims were time-barred, could not be revived by OCGA § 9-3-33.1 for acts outside Georgia, and that the revival provision violated Georgia's constitutional ban on retroactive laws and federal/state due process and equal protection clauses.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that OCGA § 9-3-33.1 can revive causes of action for childhood sexual abuse, including acts that occurred outside of Georgia, and that this does not violate Georgia's constitutional ban on retroactive laws or the Harveys' due process or equal protection rights; however, it vacated the part of the trial court's judgment regarding the statute of limitations for Quebec torts and remanded for a determination of which limitations period (Georgia's or Quebec's, if shorter) applies to those specific claims.

title: Gilliam v. State
description: Whether the Supreme Court of Georgia should retain jurisdiction over an appeal based solely on judicial economy when it otherwise lacks constitutional or statutory jurisdiction, with the plaintiff arguing for retention and the court ultimately deciding against it.
plaintiff_argument: Gilliam argued that his appeal for aggravated assault, which typically falls outside the Supreme Court's jurisdiction, should be heard by the Supreme Court alongside his co-defendant's murder conviction appeal for reasons of judicial economy.
defendant_argument: The State's argument is not explicitly detailed, but the court's decision to strictly adhere to constitutional and statutory jurisdictional limits implies a stance against expanding jurisdiction based on judicial economy.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia overruled its prior precedents that allowed it to retain jurisdiction based on judicial economy and transferred Gilliam's appeal to the Court of Appeals.

title: Duke v. State
description: Whether an indigent defendant represented by private, pro bono counsel has a statutory or constitutional right to state-funded experts and investigators needed to prepare a defense, with the plaintiff arguing they do and the defendant arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: Duke argued that as an indigent defendant, he is entitled to state-funded ancillary defense services under the Indigent Defense Act (IDA), and his choice of pro bono counsel should not impede this right to due process and a fair trial.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Duke was no longer indigent under the IDA due to his pro bono counsel, that the IDA provides no mechanism for state funding for ancillary services in such cases, and that Duke waived his right to state-funded services by choosing private counsel.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's ruling that pro bono counsel qualifies as 'other resources' and that the Indigent Defense Act provides no mechanism for indigent defendants with pro bono counsel to obtain state-funded ancillary defense services, and remanded the case for further proceedings.
